answerSnippet: Body surface area (BSA) is most often calculated with the Mosteller formula: BSA (m²) = √(weight in kg × height in cm ÷ 3600). For example, a 75 kg adult who is 175 cm tall has a BSA of about 1.91 m². The average adult BSA is 1.73 m² (women 1.6–1.8 m², men 1.8–2.0 m²). BSA is used to dose chemotherapy in mg/m² and to compute the cardiac index.
intro: **Body Surface Area (BSA)** is the total surface area of the human body, measured in **m²** (square meters). In medicine it is used to dose **chemotherapy** (mg/m²), compute the **cardiac index** (L/min/m²) and normalize the glomerular filtration rate (GFR per 1.73 m²). This calculator returns BSA with the three most accepted formulas — **Mosteller (1987)**, **Du Bois (1916)** and **Haycock (1978)** — plus their average. The **average adult has about 1.73 m²** of body surface.
keyTakeaway: The simplest and most-used formula is **Mosteller**: `BSA (m²) = √(weight × height / 3600)`. A 75 kg adult who is 175 cm tall has a BSA of about **1.91 m²**. All three formulas agree within ~2% for normal-weight adults, so any of them is reliable for dosing.

explanation:
## How to calculate body surface area

The quickest way is the **Mosteller formula** — just a square root:

```
BSA (m²) = √(weight(kg) × height(cm) / 3600)
```

## BSA reference table (Mosteller)

| Weight | Height | BSA (m²) |
|---|---|---|
| 3 kg | 50 cm | 0.20 |
| 15 kg | 95 cm | 0.63 |
| 40 kg | 150 cm | 1.29 |
| 60 kg | 165 cm | 1.66 |
| 70 kg | 170 cm | 1.82 |
| 75 kg | 175 cm | 1.91 |
| 80 kg | 180 cm | 2.00 |
| 100 kg | 185 cm | 2.27 |

## Average BSA by group

| Group | Average BSA (m²) |
|---|---|
| Newborn | 0.25 |
| 2-year-old child | 0.50 |
| 10-year-old child | 1.14 |
| Adult female | 1.60–1.80 |
| Adult male | 1.80–2.00 |
| Reference adult (GFR) | 1.73 |

## The 3 formulas

### Mosteller (1987) — most widely used today
```
BSA = √(weight(kg) × height(cm) / 3600)
```
Favored in oncology for its simplicity and accuracy.

### Du Bois & Du Bois (1916) — the original
```
BSA = 0.007184 × weight(kg)^0.425 × height(cm)^0.725
```
Derived from only 9 subjects, yet still remarkably accurate.

### Haycock (1978) — preferred in pediatrics
```
BSA = 0.024265 × weight(kg)^0.5378 × height(cm)^0.3964
```
Validated on a larger sample that included children.

## Medical applications

- **Chemotherapy**: doses are written in mg/m². Example: docetaxel 75 mg/m². If your BSA is 1.9 m², the dose is 75 × 1.9 = 142.5 mg.
- **Cardiac index**: cardiac output (L/min) ÷ BSA. Normal range: **2.5–4.0 L/min/m²**.
- **Glomerular filtration rate (GFR)**: reported per **1.73 m²** of body surface.
- **Antibiotic dosing**: e.g. vancomycin and aminoglycosides in some protocols.
- **Transplantation**: donor/recipient size compatibility.

## Differences between the formulas

For normal-weight adults the three formulas differ by **less than 2%**, so they are essentially interchangeable. Larger differences appear at the **extremes** — severe obesity, cachexia, or very small children — where Haycock tends to be preferred for pediatric patients and adjusted body weight is sometimes used in obesity.

faq.q: How do I calculate body surface area by hand?
faq.a: Use the Mosteller formula: BSA (m²) = √(weight in kg × height in cm ÷ 3600). For a 70 kg, 170 cm adult: √(70 × 170 ÷ 3600) = √3.30 = **1.82 m²**. It's the easiest formula because it only needs a square root.

faq.q: What is a normal body surface area for adults?
faq.a: The average adult BSA is about **1.73 m²** (the value used to normalize GFR). Typical ranges are **1.6–1.8 m² for women** and **1.8–2.0 m² for men**. Taller, heavier people have a larger BSA.

faq.q: Which BSA formula is most accurate?
faq.a: For adults, Mosteller, Du Bois and Haycock are all roughly equivalent (within ~2%). For **children and newborns**, Haycock is preferred. In **severe obesity** none is ideal, so some clinics dose on adjusted body weight.

faq.q: Why is body surface area used in medicine instead of just weight?
faq.a: Because BSA correlates better than weight alone with metabolic rate, blood volume and drug distribution. That's why **chemotherapy and several other drugs are dosed in mg/m²** rather than mg/kg.

faq.q: How is BSA used to calculate a chemotherapy dose?
faq.a: Chemotherapy is prescribed in **mg/m²**. Multiply the protocol dose by your BSA: if a drug is 75 mg/m² and your BSA is 1.9 m², the dose is 75 × 1.9 = **142.5 mg**. BSA is recalculated before each cycle.

faq.q: What is the cardiac index and what are normal values?
faq.a: Cardiac index is cardiac output (liters pumped per minute) divided by BSA. The normal range is **2.5–4.0 L/min/m²**. Normalizing by BSA lets clinicians compare heart function between people of different sizes.

faq.q: Can I calculate body surface area for babies and children?
faq.a: Yes. **Haycock** is the most accurate formula for newborns and children. For a 3 kg baby who is 50 cm tall, BSA ≈ **0.20 m²**; a 10-year-old averages about **1.14 m²**.

faq.q: Does body surface area change when you lose weight?
faq.a: Yes. Losing about 10 kg can lower BSA by roughly **0.1 m²**. That's why BSA is **recalculated before each chemotherapy cycle** — even small weight changes affect the dose.

faq.q: Why was the Du Bois formula based on only 9 people?
faq.a: The 1916 Du Bois & Du Bois formula was built from just 9 subjects (using paper-mold measurements), yet it has held up against modern validation studies and is still cited a century later.

faq.q: What units do the BSA formulas use?
faq.a: All three formulas here take **weight in kilograms and height in centimeters** and return BSA in **square meters (m²)**. If you have pounds or inches, convert first (1 kg = 2.205 lb, 1 in = 2.54 cm).
